entry.title: From Export to Bare Metal - The .pte Path Through pytorch/executorch

link.title: From Export to Bare Metal - The .pte Path Through pytorch/executorch

entry.content:
Every framework we have toured in this series — Triton for kernels, vLLM for throughput, MLC for cross-platform compilation — assumes you have an operating system, a Python runtime, and memory to spare. ExecuTorch, PyTorch’s edge sibling, drops all three assumptions: its target machines are microcontrollers, DSPs, and phone NPUs where your whole model must fit into a memory budget you declare in advance. The price of that constraint shapes every file in the repository, and it produces one of the cleanest ideas in inference engineering: the allocation plan is computed at export time, on a machine that has plenty of RAM, and shipped inside the artifact itself. The runtime never allocates a tensor at inference — it replays a script. This tour follows a .pte file end to end: the exir export flow that partitions, plans, and serializes it; the loader that memory-maps it; the Method that executes it one step at a time; the backend contract that hands subgraphs to vendor libraries; and the LLM runner that turns all of it into a chat loop. As always, this is an educational read of published source on the main branch, under the BSD-style license.

What makes the design worth studying is how much it refuses to do at runtime. There is no scheduler, no batcher, no memory arena hunting for blocks mid-inference — all of that was decided by a Python pass with the whole graph in view. The C++ side stays small enough to read in an afternoon, which is exactly the point for software that ships inside hearing aids and drones.

Overview of the .pte path: exir partitioners carve subgraphs to backends, the memory-planning pass assigns every tensor a spec, serialize_for_executorch writes the flatbuffer, Program loads it, Method replays the plan through the BackendInterface, and the Module plus LLM runner wrap it into an application.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • partitioner.py defines the abstract Partitioner whose call at line 66 runs partition at 75 and returns a PartitionResult with lowered subgraphs.
  • memory_planning_pass.py is where allocation becomes data: MemoryPlanningPass runs at line 280 with a multi-method variant at 346.
  • memory_planning.py computes lifetimes with update_all_tensors_lifetime and validates them through verify_storage_reuse at 165.
  • _serialize.py is the exit door: serialize_for_executorch writes the flatbuffer program and its external data segments.
  • program.cpp is the loader: Program::load verifies the file, num_methods at 353 counts entry points, and load_method at 384 builds a Method.
  • method_meta.cpp reports what a method needs — input shapes, output shapes, memory plan sizes.
  • method.cpp is the engine: Method::init wires kernels and delegates once, step at 1723 and execute at 1780 replay the plan.
  • interface.h is the vendor contract: BackendInterface with init at 84 and execute at 99.
  • module.cpp is the friendly C++ API: Module::load picks a DataLoader strategy, load_method at 543 prepares an entry point.
  • text_llm_runner.cpp is a complete chat loop: generate drives prefill at 284 and per-token decode.
  • text_decoder_runner.cpp runs one method step per token through the sampler.
  • memory_allocator.h and hierarchical_allocator.h are the bump allocators that hold every planned buffer.

Export: edge dialect, delegates, and a plan for every byte

The Python half of the repo answers a question most runtimes answer with heuristics at load time: how much memory does this model need, and where does each tensor sit? The flow starts with torch.export and a descent into the edge dialect — operator decompositions that rewrite ATen ops into the edge subset with explicit dtype and layout. Then partitioning: a backend implements the Partitioner interface, declares which ops it supports, and the exporter slices matching subgraphs out of the graph, wrapping each in a lowered module that the backend compiles however it likes. Whatever the backend cannot claim stays as a portable-kernel subgraph, so a Core ML or QNN delegate can sit beside reference C++ kernels in the same method.

The distinctive part is the planning pass. MemoryPlanningPass walks the traced graph, and for every node that materializes a tensor it attaches an allocation spec at line 229 — size, dtype, alignment, and a lifetime computed from when the tensor is last read. The core machinery in memory_planning.py collects specs from nodes, then solves a two-dimensional packing problem: tensors whose lifetimes do not overlap can share one buffer, and update_all_tensors_lifetime at line 548 supplies the intervals the packer needs. The result is a set of named memory plans — each a fixed-size pool with fixed offsets — and a verifier at line 165 that refuses to emit a program whose planned buffers overlap in invalid ways. Serialization then writes the whole story into the .pte: the flatbuffer program from serialize_for_executorch at line 44 plus constant segments laid out so a device can consume them directly. It is the same precompute-everything philosophy we saw in ONNX Runtime’s planners in the onnxruntime-2 tour, taken to its logical endpoint: not cached per input signature, but baked into the file.

Loading: segments, verification, and zero-copy

The C++ half begins with Program::load, and its first act is paranoia. The loader checks the flatbuffer identifier, verifies the whole buffer with a flatbuffers verifier, parses the extended header, and only then hands back a Program. The file is organized as segments — program, constants, mutable data — described by segment info records, and the loader never copies them: it keeps a pointer into whatever the DataLoader provided, which can be a file read, an mmap, or memory embedded at link time. PteDataMap indexes the named data so constants land where the plan expects. A Program can hold several methods — the LLM use case compiles prefill and decode as separate entry points — enumerated by num_methods at line 353 and get_method_name at 364, each loaded independently through load_method at 384, which consults method_meta for the shapes and plan sizes it must reserve.

Execution: one method, one step, one delegate call

Method::init at line 937 is where the plan meets real memory. The caller supplies a hierarchical allocator — a stack of named pools sized exactly as the export promised — and init carves every planned buffer out of those pools without a single dynamic allocation. It then walks the graph’s instructions: portable kernels are resolved by name against the registered kernel library, and each delegated subgraph is initialized through the backend’s init at line 84, which compiles the subgraph into an opaque DelegateHandle. From there, execution is a replay: Method::step at line 1723 copies inputs into their planned slots, execute at 1780 walks the instruction list — kernel calls through the EValue variant, or execute at line 99 on the backend for delegated spans — and every write lands in memory whose address was decided in Python. The TensorParser is the quiet workhorse mapping feed tensors onto the planned buffers, and the optional EventTracer records per-op spans when profiling is compiled in. The Module layer above smooths the ergonomics — its constructors at line 125 choose between FileDataLoader and mmap variants depending on the platform — and BundledModule goes one step further by linking the .pte into the application binary itself, which is how a watch face model ships with no filesystem at all.

Two supporting pieces make this machinery survivable on real hardware. The first is the DataLoader abstraction: because the loader only ever hands out borrowed views — the FreeableBuffer type wraps a pointer plus a destructor — the same Method code runs against a heap read on a laptop and against flash-mapped memory on an RTOS without caring which. The Module constructors pick the strategy per platform, trying mmap first and falling back to file reads where it is unavailable. The second is the Result type, which replaces exceptions with a value-or-error pattern throughout the runtime: every loader call, init call, and step returns one, and the absence of exception machinery keeps the binary small enough for the MCUs this code targets. Neither piece is glamorous, but together they are why the executor compiles with almost no standard library dependency — an explicit design goal you can feel in every header.

From Install to Your First Model

The LLM path ties the pieces together. TextLLMRunner owns two methods from one .pte — prefill and decode — and generate at line 74 runs prefill at 284 in chunks sized to the device, then loops TextDecoderRunner::step at line 40, which executes the decode method once, samples, appends the token, and invokes the callback. Nothing here batches across users — the whole design targets one conversation on one device, which is why the runner can stay a few hundred lines.

After pip install executorch, the knobs worth knowing are the memory ones: memory-planning modes choose between contiguous pools and per-plan pools, --memory-planning output can be inspected as a text layout, and backends like XNNPACK or Core ML register themselves as partitioners you add to the export call. Honest limits: we read the loader and method hot path, not the kernel libraries or the vendor delegates — the QNN and Core ML trees are large projects of their own. We benchmarked nothing; the zero-copy claims are structural, and real devices add alignment surprises that the dim-order passes only partially hide. And the executor is single-threaded by design — parallelism exists only inside backends. Compared with OpenVINO and ONNX Runtime, which carry their allocators and schedulers into the runtime, ExecuTorch’s answer is radical precomputation: the .pte is not just a model format, it is a memory map — and that is why the smallest devices in this series run it.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of pytorch/executorch along the whole life of a .pte file: the exir partitioners and memory-planning pass that pre-compute every tensor's address at export time, the serialized flatbuffer with its segments, Program's zero-copy loader, Method's init-once execute-per-step loop, the BackendInterface delegate contract, and the Module and LLM runner layers on top.

entry.title: Inside TurboMind: The C++ Engine Core of InternLM/lmdeploy

link.title: Inside TurboMind: The C++ Engine Core of InternLM/lmdeploy

entry.content:
Our first visit to InternLM/lmdeploy stayed above the waterline: the CLI, the lite quantization toolkit, the OpenAI-compatible server, and the fork where a request picks either the readable PyTorch engine or the compiled TurboMind core. This visit goes under the waterline, into the C++ half that EuroSys-grade numbers were built on. The questions here are the classic serving-engine questions — where do requests wait, who decides what runs next, how are KV-cache pages handed out and reused — answered with a design that is unusually clean: one engine thread that owns all mutable state, a scheduler that plans several steps ahead of the GPU, and a two-level block system where logical sequences borrow from pooled physical pages. As always, this is an educational walk through published source, Apache-2.0 licensed, on the main branch.

The design decision everything else hangs on is single-threaded ownership. Instead of locks sprinkled through the request path, TurboMind gives the engine one internal thread that pops from a Gateway, and everything else — Python, signal delivery, result forwarding — talks to that thread through queues. Reading the loop below is therefore the most direct way to understand the whole system.

The TurboMind core: the Python TurboMind class reaches through the _turbomind pybind module into the Engine; requests arrive via the Gateway, the Engine's internal thread validates, accepts, cancels and retires them, the Scheduler plans against block pools and a prefix trie, and the ModelExecutor consumes prepared BatchData on its own thread.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Python side is TurboMind: it loads weights, calls _create_engine, and hands out per-stream instances from create_instance.
  • The boundary is a pybind module: PYBIND11_MODULE exposes engine handles, request structs, and even multimodal inputs, with config classes auto-generated via a for_each trick at line 379.
  • Gateway is the doorsill: push and pop for requests, cancel for aborts, and a dedicated signal thread so notifications never block the caller.
  • The engine loop at Engine::Impl::InternalThreadEntry is the whole scheduling brain in one while-true.
  • The Scheduler plans each step: admission, prefix matching, resume versus continue, publication.
  • Blocks live in two pools — CacheBlock physical pages managed by CacheBlockPool, and LogicalBlock sequences that borrow them.

The bridge and the boundaries

Between Python and C++ sits more than a translator. The bind.cpp module defines three worlds: engine handles, the request vocabulary — requests, sequences, signals, multimodal inputs — and configuration. The configuration part is the most elegant: C++ config structs register their own fields, so a helper at lines 379 through 390 can expose every option to Python without a hand-written def per attribute — add a field to the struct and the binding follows. Multimodal inputs get first-class treatment too, with per-model item types such as QwenVitItem carrying grid dimensions and token spans, and tensor data crossing by dlpack capsule rather than by copy. On the Python side, TurboMind.init resolves the model source, _process_weights and _create_weight move tensors into the layout the kernels expect, and runtime weight updates or sleep/wakeup travel the same bridge through update_params and wakeup.

The Gateway deserves a closer look because it is the only object on the hot path that Python threads touch concurrently. push enqueues a request and wakes the signal thread; pop drains it under a free-slot budget, optionally blocking; notify is how the engine thread talks back — signals for finished, failed, or cancelled requests are handed to a separate signal thread so that a slow consumer of results never stalls the engine loop itself. Cancellation is also asynchronous: cancel marks a request, and the engine observes it in its own time, which is why the loop below has an explicit Cancel step rather than an interrupt.

The engine loop, one thread to rule the batch

InternalThreadEntry starts with pinning chores — CUDA device, a stream, allocators — then enters the loop that is the engine. Only rank zero talks to the Gateway: the pop at line 797 requests as many free slots as the batch can offer and blocks only when the batch is completely empty, a detail that keeps idle GPUs from spinning hot. The popped requests pass Validate, which checks everything the scheduler would otherwise discover mid-step — token limits, session resumption, multimodal payload shapes — and rejects early with per-request signals. Tensor-parallel ranks then synchronize at line 804 only when the batch is empty, and the full request set is broadcast so every rank runs the identical step.

The body of the iteration is a fixed order that reads like a checklist: Accept turns validated requests into sequences, Cancel applies aborts, gateway notify flushes the resulting signals, Retire frees finished sequences, and only then — with the active count re-reduced across data-parallel groups — does Schedule run. Two quiet guardians follow: FailStalledHeadOfLine catches the case where a queue head cannot fit and everything behind it starves, and cache-stats logging is throttled so observability never becomes load. The ordering matters: because retire precedes schedule, freed pages are reusable in the very same step.

The Scheduler: admission, prefixes, and partial siblings

Where the engine loop is a metronome, the Scheduler is the strategist. Each pass builds a ScheduleState and walks three phases. Required admission at line 1105 handles sequences already holding resources; optional admission at line 1219 brings new prompts in only if that cannot hurt anyone admitted. Prompt admission itself is where the KV cache gets interesting: AdmitPrompt ensures the sequence has blocks, then MatchPrompt walks the prompt against the prefix trie to find already-materialized blocks, and IndexMissingBlocks decides what must still be computed.

The subtle machinery is for shared and resumed sequences. PlanResume rehydrates a sequence from a stored session, SetupPartialSiblings splits a shared prefix where two requests diverge mid-block, and a trio — SetProducers, CheckProducers, MarkProduced — tracks which in-flight sequence will fill a block that others want, so cache reuse does not have to wait for a sequence to finish. Publication of checkpoint blocks is planned separately at PlanPublication, with a clamp that keeps a forward pass from outrunning its context. The step ends with ReplayMemory applying the plan to the block system and CommitResults handing tokens back.

Underneath the scheduler sits a small object system with real engineering in it. A LogicalBlockPtr and a CacheBlockPtr are reference-counted handles that know their pools, so release paths are exception-safe by construction. The physical pool answers the classic eviction question cheaply: SortedBlocks produces candidates in reuse-friendly order, and a Stamp computed over a set of blocks gives the trie a fingerprint to index. Lifecycle is explicit rather than implicit: Invalidate drops a block whose owner rewrote it, Deallocate returns memory to the allocator, and the logical pool’s Recycle fires the trie-erase callback that keeps the prefix index honest — the comment there even notes the pool deliberately stays prefix-agnostic.

The detail view: Python frontend and pybind bridge on the left; the engine tier of Gateway, engine loop, request structs, and BatchData; the scheduler tier with block pools, the prefix trie, and the block implementation file; the memory layer of pages and slabs underneath; and the ModelExecutor thread on the right.

Walking the detail diagram, a token’s journey touches every tier. The request struct itself is compact — Request carries inputs and a generation config, Sequence is the long-lived state, and CacheCopy records when a shared physical block must be duplicated before divergence. The block pools are pooled twice over: LogicalBlockPool recycles logical objects through a callback that erases the sequence from the prefix trie on recycle, while physical pages come from PageAllocator and the pool storage itself is slab-allocated so steady-state serving never wakes the general-purpose heap. On the other end, ModelExecutor runs its own internal thread with a Run that consumes the BatchData the engine filled — container structs like ResolvedCopy carry the block copies that must happen before attention reads.

Splitting the engine thread from the executor thread is not ceremony; it is latency hiding. The scheduler can plan step N+1 — including block allocation and copies — while the GPU is still finishing step N inside the model, and the two only meet at the BatchData hand-off. The same separation protects the reverse path: interrupts such as Interrupt mark a sequence for the engine to observe at a step boundary, and Finalize runs cleanup once the executor has drained, so a cancelled request never frees memory that attention kernels are still reading. It is the same discipline that made the single-threaded engine safe in the first place, applied one layer down.

From Install to Your First Model

Install is pip install lmdeploy, then lmdeploy serve api_server <model> picks TurboMind by default. What this tour adds is the operational reading: create_instance per stream is cheap because the engine, not the instance, owns state; the schedule metrics surfaced by get_schedule_metrics are the engine’s own counters about admission and cache pressure, worth watching before raising max_batch_size; and prefix reuse is automatic — the trie and producer tracking above are why repeated system prompts do not multiply prefill cost.

Honest limits: this walk covered the orchestration core, not the kernels — attention, MoE, and the linear layers under models/llama are their own mountain, and the PyTorch engine shares none of this C++ machinery. We read, not benchmarked; the design claims here are structural. And the engine thread model is a real contract: user code that blocks inside callbacks stalls the whole batch, which is precisely why the Gateway keeps its signal thread. For placement in the ecosystem, vLLM and SGLang solve the same block-management problem in Python, TensorRT-LLM splits the role across MPI processes, and OpenVINO shows what one-graph-per-stream looks like without any server at all. TurboMind’s answer — one thread, one plan, pooled pages — is the most conservative and arguably the easiest to reason about under load.
entry.summary: A second source tour of InternLM/lmdeploy, this time inside the TurboMind C++ core: the Gateway that ships requests across the pybind boundary, the Engine's internal thread, the Scheduler's admission and prefix-reuse machinery, pooled logical and cache blocks, and the ModelExecutor thread that turns a BatchData into a forward pass.

entry.title: Engine Actions and the Token Treadmill - The C++ Serve Core of mlc-ai/mlc-llm

link.title: Engine Actions and the Token Treadmill - The C++ Serve Core of mlc-ai/mlc-llm

entry.content:
Our first walk of mlc-ai/mlc-llm told the compile-and-serve story at the repository scale: passes that fuse weight dequantization into matmuls, quantization schemes, the async Python engine, and a note that a compact C++ core does the real work. That C++ core is where the interesting scheduling happens, and it deserves the kind of attention TurboMind got from us in the lmdeploy follow-up. Every inference loop on the planet has the same shape — pick a batch, run prefill or decode, sample, stream deltas back — and the differences between frameworks live in how each decides what a “step” is, how requests move between queues, and what happens when you want to draft five tokens and throw four away. mlc-llm answers all three with an unusually clean vocabulary: one background thread, a step function that selects exactly one EngineAction per iteration, and a request-state machine whose draft token slots make speculative decoding a bookkeeping exercise rather than a special case. As always, this is an educational read of published Apache-2.0 source on the main branch; the first post at /mlc-llm/ covers the compiler side we deliberately skip here.

The architectural headline is that the whole serving engine is a two-thread conversation. Requests arrive from Python as instructions into a queue owned by the background thread; the background thread runs step after step, and every delta — every new token — flows back through a callback loop into Python without either thread ever blocking the other. Everything else in cpp/serve exists to keep that conversation moving: the actions are the verbs, the state is the ledger, and the sampler is the arithmetic.

Overview of the serve core: Python engines hand instructions to the ThreadedEngine, its background loop drives EngineImpl's step dispatcher, the EngineAction family covers prefill, decode, and speculative paths, EngineState and RequestState track every request, and the prefix cache plus GPU sampler close the loop.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • engine_base.py is the Python side of the callback bridge: the async stream callback turns C++ deltas into asyncio wakeups, with a sync twin at line 548.
  • sync_engine.py exposes add_request and an explicit step for callers who want to own the loop.
  • threaded_engine.cc owns RunBackgroundLoop and RunBackgroundStreamBackLoop, fed by an instruction queue at line 356.
  • engine.cc is the dispatcher: EngineImpl::Step, beside AddRequest at line 668 and HandleSpecialRequests at 535.
  • engine_state.cc keeps the queues and hands out per-request states plus the running-state list at 33.
  • action.h declares the entire action vocabulary in one line: Step takes the state and returns finished requests.
  • new_request_prefill.cc starts running requests; batch_decode.cc keeps them running one token at a time.
  • auto_spec_decode.cc routes between draft, verify, and jump-forward when a draft model is configured.
  • request_state.cc is the ledger: CommitToken, RollbackTokens at 70, AddDraftToken at 85.
  • prefix_cache.cc reuses work through ExtendSequence, RollBackSequence at 177, and RecycleSequence at 191.
  • gpu_sampler.cc does the arithmetic: top-p renormalization and batched sampling at 190.
  • logit_processor.cc shapes logits before sampling with bias, penalties, and grammar masks.

A step is an action

The design’s one big idea is easiest to see in the dispatcher. EngineImpl::Step does no model work itself: it checks whether there are new requests to absorb or dead requests to clean, picks exactly one action object, calls its Step, and hands the returned list of finished request ids to the state for cleanup. Which action gets picked is a matter of one if-chain: if any waiting request can join the batch, prefill; if a speculative configuration is active, the speculative action; otherwise decode. Each action is a self-contained class. NewRequestPrefillActionObj::Step walks the waiting queue, consults the prefix cache for reusable blocks, and packs as many prompts as fit into a chord-shaped prefill batch. BatchDecodeActionObj::Step is the treadmill’s heartbeat: it assembles the running batch, runs one forward step on the model, then samples the whole batch in one call at line 170. Underneath both, function_table.cc is the FFI registry that made the model callable: Init and _InitFunctions at 207 load the TVM runtime functions — prefill, decode, kv cache ops — that every action calls by name, and CopyToWorker0 shuttles host data to the device. Where actions need each other’s plumbing, action_commons.cc shares the batch-assembly and output-merge helpers rather than duplicating them.

The two-thread story is what makes this elegant rather than merely neat. Python calls into ThreadedEngine only to push an instruction — add request, abort request, reload — and the instruction queue at line 356 is the single crossing point. The background loop drains it, runs steps, and parks deltas in an output queue; the stream-back loop at 191 waits on that queue and fires the callback into Python. Two condition variables, no locks held during model execution, and the vtable at line 386 is the whole surface Python ever sees. It is a lighter pattern than the process-per-worker lattice we mapped in TensorRT-LLM, and it means a reload never tears down the Python event loop.

The lifecycle bookkeeping around that loop is worth its own paragraph, because it shows how much production reality the dispatcher absorbs. Engine construction is Engine::Create at line 1016, which funnels through AutoDecideEngineConfig at line 893 — the stage that fills in defaults the user left blank and picks a mode single-GPU versus speculative versus disaggregated. Requests that are not ordinary completions are intercepted before they reach the queues: HandleSpecialRequests at line 535 answers debug and control instructions inline, and HandleDisaggRequest at line 553 recognizes requests that arrived from a remote prefill node in disaggregated serving. Failures stream back through the same callback as successes — StreamBackError at line 529 wraps an error and a finish reason into a normal-looking delta so the Python side never needs a second error channel. On the far side of the bridge, process_chat_completion_request at line 687 is where OpenAI-shaped JSON becomes a C++ Request, and its stream-output twin at line 781 converts deltas back into chat-completions chunks. The wire dialect changes nothing in the core — which is precisely the point of the layering.

Speculative drafts and the state machine

Speculative decoding is where this architecture pays off. Without a draft model, a step is a decode. With one, AutoSpecDecodeActionObj::Step becomes a tiny state machine of its own: it alternates BatchDraftActionObj::Step, where the small model commits a block of k draft tokens per request, with BatchVerifyActionObj::Step, where the large model runs all drafts in parallel and the sampler accepts the longest correct prefix. A jump-forward action at line 36 handles the structured-output case — when a grammar or a JSON schema says the next five characters are already decided, the engine jumps them without a forward pass at all. The EAGLE path swaps in different actions — eagle_batch_draft.cc and eagle_batch_verify.cc — with feature vectors and tree-shaped verification, and the dispatcher at line 78 wraps whichever family you configured.

What makes draft-then-verify cheap to reason about is the request state. RequestModelStateNode::AddDraftToken parks each draft in a numbered slot; CommitToken records accepted tokens and RollbackTokens rewinds the ones the verifier rejected, with RemoveAllDraftTokens reporting which KV cache slots to recycle. The same ledger serves non-speculative paths: grammar-constrained decoding asks for a token bitmask at line 48, and every streamed delta is composed by GetDeltaRequestReturn at line 175. The sampler underneath is quietly sophisticated: BatchRenormalizeProbsByTopP renormalizes on-device before BatchSampleTokensWithProbAfterTopP at line 190 draws from the surviving mass, and GenerateUniformSamples at line 480 pre-generates random numbers on GPU so the per-request RNG state never round-trips through the host. Bias and penalties arrive earlier through InplaceUpdateLogits, UpdateWithPenalty at 270, and UpdateWithMask at 372.

The prefix cache underneath

Serving quality often depends on what you do not recompute, and this repo’s answer is a paged radix tree in C++. PrefixCacheImpl exposes four operations: ExtendSequence claims blocks for growing tokens, CommitSequenceExtention at 154 makes a speculative extension durable, RollBackSequence at 177 releases the tail after verification rewinds, and RecycleSequence at 191 marks a finished conversation for lazy reuse. The tree itself, radix_tree.cc, indexes sequences at block granularity so two conversations sharing a system prompt share those KV blocks for free — the same idea we saw in SGLang’s radix cache and in the Python-side tree the first tour showed, now living close to the C++ actions that use it. TryFreeMemory at line 225 is the pressure valve that evicts leaves when a new prefill needs room.

From Install to Your First Model

None of this needs configuration: python -m mlc_llm serve builds it and runs it, and create_sync or AsyncThreadedEngine expose the same core in-process. The visible knobs are speculative — a draft model plus spec decode mode flips the action dispatcher — and the debug surface: the event trace recorder emits per-request spans you can read in Chrome’s trace viewer, which is the fastest way to see the prefill-chord and draft-verify alternation in a real log.

Honest limits: we read the single-GPU path; disaggregated prefill and decode across nodes exists in the same actions folder but we did not trace it, and the embedding engine shares none of this. The sampler reads correct but we benchmarked nothing — top-p behavior on GPU is exactly where silent numerical drift hides. And the action set is still growing; jump-forward and EAGLE both landed recently, which is why this layer rewards a second reading. For context: vLLM solves speculative decoding at the Python scheduler layer, SGLang shares the radix-tree idea from the same lineage, LM Studio-style local stacks wrap engines rather than reimplement them, and LocalAI routes to backends it does not own. mlc-llm’s one-action-per-step C++ core is the most legible of these — you can hold the whole token treadmill in your head, which is exactly why it was worth a second visit.
entry.summary: A second source tour of mlc-ai/mlc-llm, this time inside the C++ serve core: the ThreadedEngine's two background loops, EngineImpl's step dispatcher, the EngineAction family from prefill to decode to speculative draft and verify, the request state machine with its draft slots and rollbacks, the GPU sampler's top-p machinery, and the radix-tree prefix cache underneath.

entry.title: From Run() to Buffers - The ONNX Runtime Execution Machinery

link.title: From Run() to Buffers - The ONNX Runtime Execution Machinery

entry.content:
Our first walk of microsoft/onnxruntime stayed at the architectural level: the versioned C API, the fusion transformers, MLAS, the CUDA provider, and the training stack. That post ends where every session ends up on a hot path — a call to Run() with a dictionary of feeds — and leaves the most performance-critical half of the codebase unexplored: what actually happens between that call and the last kernel’s write. This tour follows exactly that half. It is a story with three distinct layers. At the top, InferenceSession::RunImpl validates options and hands the plan to an executor. In the middle, ExecuteThePlan walks the graph across a small set of device streams, checking barriers before each node fires. At the bottom, an ExecutionFrame and a best-fit-coalescing arena have already pre-computed — at session initialization time — where every byte of every intermediate tensor will live, so that a steady-state inference run performs almost no allocator decision-making at all. As always in this series, this is an educational read of published MIT-licensed source on the main branch; the first post at /onnxruntime/ covers the API surface and provider layer that this machinery serves.

The headline is that ONNX Runtime treats allocation as a compile-time problem, not a runtime one. Two planners run during Initialize, not during inference: one assigns nodes and weights to devices, the other traces every buffer’s lifetime and folds the resulting sizes into reusable memory patterns. By the time Run() is called, the expensive questions have yes-or-no answers cached in the session state, and the per-run work reduces to bookkeeping — which is why the code can afford a comparatively elegant stream walk in the middle.

Overview of the execution machinery: RunImpl enters the executor, ExecuteThePlan walks nodes through the StreamExecutionContext and DeviceStreamCollection down to device handles like CudaStream, the planners and ExecutionFrame pre-compute every allocation into the BFCArena, and KernelRegistryManager plus the Memcpy kernel and the ThreadPool round out the launch path.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • inference_session.cc is the public face: Load for file paths, RunImpl for the hot path, and RunAsync at 4141 for the callback variant.
  • sequential_executor.cc holds ExecuteThePlan and ExecuteKernel — the modern stream-based execution loop that replaced the old class-based executors.
  • stream_execution_context.cc defines the per-run context whose constructor starts at line 12, with DecCountDownBarrier enforcing launch order.
  • device_stream_collection.cc builds one stream per EP stream id: SetDeviceStream fills the set, GetStreamForDevice looks it back up.
  • cuda_stream_handle.cc is the concrete NVIDIA handle: EnqueDeferredCPUBuffer and CleanUpOnRunEnd manage host-side work on device time.
  • allocation_planner.cc at 2600+ lines contains PlannerImpl::CreatePlan and the DeviceBasedPartitioner.
  • ort_value_pattern_planner.cc traces lifetimes through TraceAllocation and emits GeneratePatterns.
  • execution_frame.cc materializes buffers per run: AllocateAsPerAllocationPlan follows the precomputed recipe.
  • bfc_arena.cc is the best-fit-coalescing allocator — Alloc, SplitChunk, Merge, and a stream-aware variant at line 850.
  • kernel_registry_manager.cc resolves ops to kernels: SearchKernelRegistry and CreateKernel.
  • memcpy.cc is the tiny Memcpy::Compute kernel that bridges devices.
  • threadpool.cc implements ParallelForFixedBlockSizeScheduling over the Eigen-derived work-stealing pool.

Before anything runs: kernels, plans, and the fallback

Initialization is where the engine earns its steady state. After the graph transforms have fused and rewritten the model — the subject of the first tour — SessionState::FinalizeSessionState locks in three artifacts. First, kernels: SessionState::CreateKernels asks the KernelRegistryManager to construct a kernel instance per node, and that manager’s SearchKernelRegistry walks every registered registry comparing op, version, type constraints, and execution-provider capability until one matches. This is why a session cannot gain provider support mid-run: the kernel objects were built for one specific partition, with attributes and constant initializers already attached. Second, plans. PlannerImpl::CreatePlan runs the topological walk twice, essentially — once to assign every node to a device via the DeviceBasedPartitioner, deciding where weights and activations will live, and once to build the per-node allocation recipe. Where a provider cannot claim a node, GetCpuPreferredNodes keeps the CPU EP from over-reaching by preferring nodes whose weights are small enough to matter and whose placement would not trigger a cascade of copies.

Third, memory patterns. The OrtValuePatternPlanner replays the plan in miniature: every TraceAllocation and TraceFree records a buffer’s lifetime, and GeneratePatterns folds them into a MemoryPatternGroup — a block layout in which activations that never overlap can share one arena region. The session state caches these groups keyed on the shapes of the input tensors: UpdateMemoryPatternGroupCache stores the first match it computes, and ResolveMemoryPatternFlag decides whether patterns are even legal, which depends on whether the model has run-to-run shape variability. Fixed-batch deployments — the common inference server case — hit the cached pattern on run two and reuse it forever. This is the same weight-reuse philosophy we saw in the TurboMind block manager of lmdeploy-2, just expressed in C++ allocator terms instead of token-block terms.

One run, many streams

The executor itself is refreshingly small once the precomputation is done. ExecuteThePlan builds a fresh ExecutionFrame, feeds the inputs, and drives the node loop; ExecuteKernel is the per-node body that resolves OrtValues, wraps them in a kernel context, and calls Compute. What makes this loop modern is that it is stream-first: the engine no longer pretends there is one global execution thread. Instead, DeviceStreamCollection holds one stream per logical execution lane — typically one per device, plus extra ones a model may have declared with a loop or an if — and SetDeviceStream wires concrete handles into those lanes at run start. A run that touches two devices gets two lanes; a node on lane A that consumes a tensor produced on lane B must wait for a notification, and that is exactly what the StreamExecutionContext tracks with its notification table and countdown barriers.

The abstraction that keeps this device-neutral lives in stream_handles.h: a Stream with CreateNotification and Flush, and a Notification the consumer can wait on. The framework ships a default implementation in plugin_ep_stream.cc — its WaitNotificationOnDevice is an honest placeholder that busy-waits on host — and providers override it. The CUDA override is the instructive one: CudaStream wraps a cudaStream_t, and its CreateNotification produces a real event-based cross-lane wait. The subtle piece is host-side work: when a kernel needs to write a value that only becomes known mid-run (a shape, a dynamic dimension), the CUDA path cannot block the device, so EnqueDeferredCPUBuffer parks the host buffer in a queue that CleanUpOnRunEnd drains after the stream has actually finished — the DeferredCpuAllocator at line 11 exists to make that buffering transparent to the caller. Cross-lane data movement itself is just a node: the Memcpy kernel gets inserted by the planner wherever a consumer’s device differs from its producer’s, and GetStreamForDevice decides which lane executes it.

The frame and the arena: where every byte comes from

On the first run with a new input signature, the ExecutionFrame earns its keep. IExecutionFrame::Init binds feeds to OrtValue slots; AllocateMLValueTensorSelfOwnBuffer handles the naive case where a tensor owns its own buffer; and AllocateAsPerAllocationPlan handles the fast case — it consults the precomputed plan, and when a memory pattern exists, every activation in the group is carved out of a single arena reservation at fixed offsets. CreateNodeOutputMLValueImpl then hands those regions to the kernels as writable tensors, and ExecutionFrame::GeneratePatterns is the bridge that turns a planner’s group into real buffer geometry. Underneath all of it sits the arena. BFCArena — best-fit with coalescing, the same design PyTorch’s caching allocator made famous — takes big chunks from the device allocator via Extend, splits them through SplitChunk into size-ordered bins, and rejoins freed neighbors through Merge. The payoff shows up on the second run: Free returns blocks to bins instead of the device, so steady-state inference does zero device allocator calls for activations. The stream-aware variant at AllocOnStream sharpens this per lane, and when memory pressure bites, DumpMemoryLog prints the bin-by-bin accounting that turns “why is my GPU OOM” into an answer.

The last layer is concurrency inside kernels themselves. Most heavy kernels do not monoprocess their input; they chop it into blocks and call ParallelForFixedBlockSizeScheduling on the intra-op pool, which schedules fixed-size chunks across worker threads with the deterministic block ordering the profiler-facing ThreadPoolProfiler machinery records. The pool is a vendored, heavily modified Eigen work-stealing pool: ThreadPoolTempl drives lock-free queues implemented as the spsc RunQueue at line 495, with the ThreadPoolLoop shim at line 403 bridging to Eigen’s own primitives. So a GEMM on CPU is three systems deep — the MLAS kernel from the first tour, the pool feeding its blocks, and the arena holding its operands — and all three were shaped by the same decision: do the expensive thinking once, at Initialize, so Run() only executes.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything above is on by default after pip install onnxruntime or onnxruntime-gpu. The knobs that expose the machinery: session options control intra-op and inter-op thread counts, arena settings like arena_extend_strategy choose between growing the arena in kArenaAllocation steps and reusing device allocator memory, and enable_mem_pattern toggles the whole pattern system for debugging. When a run behaves oddly, ORT_DEBUG_NODE_IO and the memory-pattern dump give the two most direct windows into this layer — the arena’s DumpMemoryLog output is genuinely one of the most readable allocator reports in the ecosystem.

Honest limits: this walk focused on the CPU-plus-CUDA path because that is where the code is complete; the WebGPU, NNAPI, and Core ML providers implement the same Stream/Notification contracts with their own quirks that we did not read. We read code, not benchmarks — the “allocation is pre-computed” claim is structural, but real-world wins depend on shape stability, and a model with dynamic batch sizes will spend its runs in the slower self-owned-buffer branch. And the executor is mid-migration: the old class-based executors are gone, the stream-based loop above is the present, and the training stack shares it with extensions we deliberately skipped. For context: vLLM and SGLang solve the same memory-recycling problem at the request level with paged KV blocks, TensorRT-LLM precomputes allocation inside an engine build step, and OpenVINO answers on CPU with its own plugin allocator scheme. ONNX Runtime’s answer — plan once, pattern-cache, arena-recycle, stream-barrier — is the most explicit and most inspectable of the lot, which is exactly why it rewards this second reading.
entry.summary: A second source tour of microsoft/onnxruntime focused on what happens after you call Run: ExecuteThePlan's stream-based walk, the StreamExecutionContext that sequence-checks node launches, DeviceStreamCollection and the CUDA stream handles behind it, the planners that pre-compute every allocation, the BFCArena that recycles buffers across runs, and the Eigen-derived thread pools inside the kernels.

entry.title: From Python Call to cuLaunchKernelEx - The Triton Launch Path

link.title: From Python Call to cuLaunchKernelEx - The Triton Launch Path

entry.content:
Our first walk of openai/triton followed the compiler’s front door: how a decorated Python function becomes an AST, then TTIR, then the GPU-shaped dialects, then PTX or GCN. That leaves the other half of the story untouched — the part that runs every single frame, not just once per shape. When vLLM or a torch.compile’d model calls kernel[grid](args) for the ten-thousandth time, no compilation happens at all. What happens instead is one of the most carefully tuned hot paths in the Python ecosystem: a generated binder re-packs the arguments, a two-level cache turns the call into a key, a launch-metadata lazily assembles only if a profiler is watching, and a per-target launcher finally hands the whole thing to a small C extension that speaks the CUDA driver API directly. This tour follows that path end to end, from JITFunction.run in Python to cuLaunchKernelEx in C, with a stop in the NVIDIA backend to see how much of the compile decision is already settled by compute capability. As always, this is an educational read of published source on the main branch, under the MIT license; the earlier post at /triton/ covers the frontend and the MLIR dialects.

The headline is how much of the design is organized around one fact: on a healthy system, the cache-hit branch of run() must be nearly free. Everything else — the binder generated at import time, metadata packed once into a tuple, handles loaded lazily exactly once, hooks that short-circuit to None when no profiler is attached — serves that goal.

The launch path: JITFunction.run consults the per-device binder and kernel cache, a miss goes through CompiledKernel into the CUDABackend's stage sequence and the C++ MLIR lowering, while a hit goes straight to the launcher created in _init_handles — the CudaLauncher that forwards to driver.c and cuLaunchKernelEx.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • JITFunction.run is the hot entry: binder call, cache key, launch. The binder itself is generated from the signature, and one exists per device in device_caches.
  • FileCacheManager persists compile artifacts in hash-keyed directories.
  • CompiledKernel holds the per-stage artifacts and loads CUDA module and function handles lazily in _init_handles.
  • CUDABackend owns the stage sequence and every capability-gated option.
  • The C++ side lowers TritonGPU IR in ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM, with shared-memory allocation computed per layout conversion.
  • CudaLauncher builds argument metadata and forwards everything to the launch function in driver.c.

The hit path: one binder, two caches, three guards

run() starts by fetching the current device and stream — two driver calls that later decide which cache to use. Then comes the binder: a function created once by create_function_from_signature that binds arguments, classifies constants, and produces the specialization tuple in a single pass of straight Python. Its output feeds compute_cache_key, and the key is looked up in the kernel cache. Only a miss reaches _do_compile and the _pack_args path where backend options are parsed. This is the quiet half of Triton’s speed: the expensive work of understanding a Python signature happens once per device, not once per launch.

Even the cache-hit branch runs guards, and each one exists because someone got burned. Lines 773 through 776 re-read every global variable the kernel captured and raise if one changed — without this, editing a constant in a notebook would silently keep using the old value baked into the binary. The grid canonicalization accepts callables so a kernel can compute its own launch size from the bound arguments, defaulting missing dims to 1. And the final launch at lines 788 through 789 passes launch_metadata — built by a method that returns None immediately when no launch hook is installed, so the profiling path costs nothing when nobody is listening.

CompiledKernel: lazy handles and one launcher per source

The object the cache stores is deliberately inert. Its constructor reads the metadata JSON, restores the target from a dict into a GPUTarget, packs the metadata once via the backend’s pack_metadata — on NVIDIA that is just the tuple (num_warps, num_ctas, shared) — and loads every compilation stage’s text into an AsmDict: ttir, ttgir, llir, ptx, and the cubin bytes. What it deliberately does not do is touch the driver. module, function, and _run start as None, and only the run property triggers _init_handles, which instantiates the backend launcher class, checks the kernel’s shared-memory request against the device maximum, checks tensor-memory limits on Blackwell, and finally calls load_binary to get a CUfunction plus register and spill counts. Even failure is engineered: the raise_ helper deep-copies the exception into a closure so a cached kernel that always fails does not keep its whole traceback alive in the global cache.

There is a second, lower-level entry for people who want to launch without the JIT machinery at all: CompiledKernel.getitem returns a plain runner closure taking raw grid and stream — the escape hatch that serving frameworks use when they want to manage streams themselves.

Capability decides: CUDABackend’s stage sequence

The NVIDIA backend opens with an opinion worth quoting in spirit: its constructor stores the numeric compute capability and sets the binary extension to cubin. Everything downstream branches on that integer. parse_options turns sanitizers on debug mode, forces max_occupancy=1 under the gsan instrumentation, refuses the clc option below SM100, refuses multi-CTA below SM90, extends the supported fp8 set at capability 89 and above, and defaults Hopper’s imprecise-accumulator ceiling. The make_ttgir sequence reads like a generation table: after the convert-to-TTGIR pass, Ampere gets a prefetch pass at line 358; the Hopper branch at lines 328 through 337 adds warp specialization with latency assignment and loop scheduling for software pipelining; the Blackwell branch at lines 338 through 353 hoists tensor-memory allocations, promotes operands to tmem, and runs warp specialization again over partitioned warps. Common tail: TMA lowering at line 364, fence insertion at line 374, MMA lowering at line 375.

The back half of compilation leaves MLIR entirely. make_ptx calls LLVM’s translate-to-asm, then regex-finds the single .visible .entry name for the metadata, rewrites the .version and .target lines to the chosen PTX and SM, and strips the debug flag that would stop ptxas from optimizing. make_cubin writes the PTX to a temp file and shells out to ptxas — a real external binary resolved per architecture — with line-info only by default, --fmad=false when fp fusion is disabled, and a pinned register-allocation level that works around a ptxas 13.x bug. It is a sobering reminder that this “Python compiler” ends with string rewriting and a subprocess.

The detail view: the runtime tier of JITFunction, caches, knobs, and the user allocator; the compile tier of CompiledKernel and the AST code generator; the backend of CUDABackend, CudaLauncher, and driver.c; the C++ lowering of the LLVM conversion pass and its pattern families; and the allocation and barrier passes underneath.

Walking the detail diagram, the compile leg crosses the C++ boundary at ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM, whose populateConversionPatterns wires in the NVIDIA pattern families: layout conversions with swizzling, tensor-map creation and the fenceproxy-acquire that TMA descriptors require, fp8 and fp16 cast sequences for elementwise ops, and the heavyweight LoadStoreOpToLLVM, whose atomic-RMW conversion even promotes atomics to plain load-acquire when the access pattern allows it. Before any of that runs, the AllocateSharedMemoryNv pass has already decided which conversions need scratch space and where each byte sits. On the runtime side, global and profile scratch buffers come from the user allocator registered with set_allocator — a deliberately tiny protocol, with a null allocator that raises a helpful message when a kernel needs scratch and nobody registered one.

The last hop: CudaLauncher and the C extension

The launcher is built per compiled kernel. CudaLauncher.init decides between the TMA argument ABI and a decomposed one based on whether tensor descriptors appear in the metadata, injects three extra signature entries when the gsan instrumentation is on, and — quietly one of the neatest tricks in the file — computes a shared-memory budget: when a kernel was compiled with a max_occupancy request, lines 267 through 279 round the per-CTA budget down to 128-byte units and subtract the driver’s reserved shared memory, so compilation stays device-independent while launch-time reservation does not. It then builds the argument metadata once through the C extension and wraps the extension’s launch function, optionally with a tensordesc wrapper.

The call allocates global scratch through the user allocator and profile scratch through either the profiler’s allocator or a default one, refuses to run gsan kernels under CUDA graph capture, and re-packs the metadata tuple with the resolved shared size before crossing into C. The C side, driver.c, loaded the cubin with cuModuleLoadData back in _init_handles; at launch it builds a CUlaunchConfig whose grid X is multiplied by the CTA count and whose block X is 32 times the warp count, then attaches up to four launch attributes as needed: an oversized-shared-memory mode above 228 KB, programmatic dependent launch, cooperative launch, and cluster dimensions plus a spread scheduling policy, with a non-portable allowance when sixteen CTAs per cluster are requested. One call to cuLaunchKernelEx at line 1075 and the kernel is running.

From Install to Your First Model

After pip install triton, nothing above needs configuration — but the knobs make the layers visible. knobs.runtime.launch_enter_hook and its exit twin are what profilers attach to, and the whole launch_metadata machinery exists so those hooks can see grid, stream, and arguments without paying for it otherwise; TRITON_INTERPRET=1 swaps the compiled path for the pure-Python interpreter covered in the first tour. The observable side effects of this tour are in CompiledKernel objects themselves: n_regs and n_spills from ptxas, metadata.shared from the allocation pass, and the per-stage IR strings in asm — the same artifacts the disk cache persists.

Honest limits: this walk deliberately stayed on the NVIDIA path — the AMD backend mirrors the same stage structure with its own GCN-lowering tree, and the interpreter and Gluon paths diverge from the launcher story entirely. We read code, not benchmarks; the “nearly free” claim about the hit path is structural, not measured. And the launch surface moves fast — attribute handling, tensor descriptors, and the scratch protocol all grew within the last year, which is exactly why this layer rewards a second reading. For context in the ecosystem: vLLM and SGLang spend their days inside the hot path described here, TensorRT-LLM replaces the launcher with a full process lattice, and OpenVINO answers the same “compile once, launch cheaply” question on CPU. Triton’s answer — a generated binder, a tuple of packed metadata, and four launch attributes away from the driver — is the leanest of the lot.
entry.summary: A second source tour of openai/triton focused on what happens when you actually call a kernel: the per-device binder and kernel cache in JITFunction.run, CompiledKernel's lazy CUDA handles, the capability-driven CUDABackend stages from TTGIR to cubin, the C++ MLIR lowering to LLVM, and the CudaLauncher that finally reaches cuLaunchKernelEx with PDL, cooperative, and cluster attributes.

entry.title: The Recipe Book Behind Zephyr and SmolLM3 - Inside huggingface/alignment-handbook

link.title: The Recipe Book Behind Zephyr and SmolLM3 - Inside huggingface/alignment-handbook

entry.content:
Some repositories impress with volume, and some with restraint. The Alignment Handbook, from Lewis Tunstall, Edward Beeching, Nathan Lambert, Nazneen Rajani, Shengyi Huang, Kashif Rasul, Alvaro Bartolome, Carlos M. Patino, Alexander M. Rush, and Thomas Wolf at Hugging Face, is emphatically the second kind. It is the codebase that produced Zephyr-7B-beta - one of the most downloaded fine-tuned chat models of its moment on the Hub - and later the post-training recipe behind SmolLM3-3B, yet its entire Python surface is barely 1,250 lines: three launch scripts that mostly wire arguments together, a four-module support package, and one test file. The real payload is the recipes directory: versioned YAML files that record every hyperparameter, dataset split, and accelerate setting behind each released model, with a technical report at arXiv 2310.16944 documenting the results.

As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: accelerate configs and Slurm launchers feed the three training scripts; a thin alignment package validates dataset mixtures and loads models; each script wraps one TRL trainer; recipe YAMLs drive everything; release tooling ships checkpoints to the Hub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • scripts/sft.py is the 174-line supervised fine-tuning entry point: main at line 54 loads data at 87, tokenizer at 91, and model at 96, falls back to ChatML when the tokenizer has no template at 98-100, and builds TRL’s SFTTrainer at 105-112.
  • scripts/dpo.py, 159 lines, builds the policy and a second frozen reference model with two get_model calls at lines 100-101, then hands both to DPOTrainer at 122-130 - the same implicit-reward loss we toured in direct-preference-optimization, now production-wrapped.
  • scripts/orpo.py, 158 lines, is the single-stage variant: ORPOTrainer at line 122 takes no reference model, fusing SFT and preference alignment into one run.
  • src/alignment/configs.py extends TRL’s argument dataclasses: DatasetConfig at line 37, DatasetMixtureConfig at 48, and ScriptArguments at 57 whose post_init at 88 validates mixtures and enforces consistent column sets at 122-130.
  • src/alignment/data.py is the 79-line heart of the mixture API: get_dataset at line 26 loads each entry, subsamples by weight at 52-56, concatenates and reshuffles at 61-62, and optionally carves a test split at 65-68.
  • src/alignment/model_utils.py holds get_tokenizer at line 23 - which can override the chat template at 31-32 - and get_model at 37, resolving dtype and quantization at 39-42 and disabling the KV cache under gradient checkpointing at 48.
  • recipes/zephyr-7b-beta/dpo/config_full.yaml is the artifact that made the repo famous: it starts from the SFT checkpoint, mixes ultrafeedback_binarized preference splits, and sets beta 0.01 with learning rate 5e-7.
  • recipes/smollm3/sft/sft.yaml is the modern extreme: 228 lines declaring 26 weighted smoltalk2 sources, packing with the ffd strategy at length 65536, assistant-only loss, and five epochs.

Why You Need This

Frameworks are places where options go to hide. LLaMA-Factory and axolotl expose hundreds of switches because they must serve every use case; the Handbook inverts that - it serves exactly one use case, replicating published results, and strips everything else away. Each script is a legible main function you can read top to bottom in two minutes: set seed, load data, load tokenizer, load model, construct trainer, train, save, push. Where ms-swift routes dozens of model families through registries and OpenRLHF distributes a controller over Ray, the Handbook’s entire distribution story is three accelerate config files and a 176-line Slurm script. Reading it teaches you what a TRL training run actually consists of when no framework is watching.

The mixture API deserves its own study because data blending turned out to be the quiet superpower of every model this repo shipped. The Zephyr SFT recipe mixes ultrachat_200k train and test splits with equal weights; the SmolLM3 recipe blends 26 sources with weights from 1.0 down to 0.02, balancing everyday chats against function calling, long-context tasks, and reasoning traces in both think and no-think variants. The implementation is deliberately simple - shuffle, take a weight fraction, concatenate, reshuffle - and tests/test_data.py pins the arithmetic: three 100-row datasets weighted 0.5, 0.3, and 0.2 yield exactly 90 train and 10 test rows, asserted at lines 44-45. If you have ever wondered how recipe authors express “mostly instruction data, a dash of math,” this is the answer, and it transfers directly to your own training runs, whether you fine-tune full weights with deepspeed ZeRO-3 or bolt peft adapters on through the same get_peft_config call at sft.py line 111.

Finally, the Handbook is the missing link between the algorithm papers this series has covered and the models you actually download. The DPO recipe here is the industrial version of the reference implementation - same loss, but with checkpoint resumption, Hub push, model cards tagged alignment-handbook at sft.py line 145, and the generation config’s eos_token_id synced to the tokenizer at lines 136-137 to prevent unbounded generation. The ORPO script shows the alternative trade - skip the reference model entirely - while the evaluation guidance in scripts/README.md points at MT-Bench, AlpacaEval, and Chatbot Arena, a reminder that lm-evaluation-harness scores are only one lens on a chat model. The repo even ships its own release tooling, because a recipe you cannot re-version is a recipe you cannot trust.

Detail: three script mains share the parser, mixture API, and model loaders; each wraps a different TRL trainer; recipe YAMLs parameterize everything from Zephyr’s two stages to SmolLM3’s 26-corpus blend; release tooling closes the versioning loop.

The scripts are deliberately near-identical, and the diffs are where the interesting decisions live. All three begin with set_seed at line 56 (sft.py), checkpoint detection via get_last_checkpoint at 78-82, and the same three-part TrlParser at the bottom - ScriptArguments, a task config, and TRL’s ModelConfig - so every recipe is one YAML deep. sft.py’s signature moves: when the tokenizer lacks a chat template, setup_chat_format retrofits the model’s embedding matrix for ChatML special tokens at 98-100; before saving, eos_token_id is written into both generation_config and config at 136-137; and on the main process only, use_cache is switched back on at 150-151 since training disabled it for gradient checkpointing. dpo.py instead builds two models - policy at line 100, reference at 101 - falls back to eos as the pad token at 103-104, carries an ignore_bias_buffers switch at 105-109 that tells DDP to skip boolean buffers (a workaround for Flash Attention asserts in distributed DPO), and strips the messages column at 114-117 so the trainer sees only chosen/rejected pairs. orpo.py removes the reference model altogether, matching the method’s single-stage design documented in its docstring with max_length 2048.

The mixture chain is three short files acting in concert. ScriptArguments at configs.py line 57 accepts either dataset_name or a dataset_mixture dict; post_init at 88 rejects configs with neither, coerces the raw dict into DatasetConfig entries at 99-112 - each carrying id, config name, split, a columns whitelist, and a weight - and then insists at 122-130 that every entry whitelists the same column names, because concatenation would otherwise fail late and cryptically. get_dataset in data.py takes it from there: the single-dataset branch at lines 35-37 is a plain load_dataset call, while the mixture branch at 38-76 loads each source with its split at 45-49, applies select_columns at 50-51, implements weights as shuffle-then-select(range(int(len(ds) * weight))) at 52-56, concatenates at 61, applies one final seeded shuffle at 62, and either returns a DatasetDict with a train_test_split at 65-68 or wraps everything as a lone train split at 73-74. The tests lock the semantics in at three weight regimes, including the fractional case where 70 plus 40 rows become 99 train and 11 test at lines 87-105.

The model layer is fifty-seven lines that encode real distributed-training judgment. get_tokenizer at model_utils.py line 23 loads with the model revision and trust_remote_code flags from ModelConfig, then applies the recipe’s chat_template override at 31-32 - which is how Zephyr’s custom template and SmolLM3’s reasoning-aware template, both stored as YAML strings inside the recipes, reach the tokenizer without any code changes. get_model at line 37 resolves torch_dtype from the string at 39-41, asks TRL for a bitsandbytes quantization config at 42, and assembles model_kwargs at 43-51: attention implementation passthrough, use_cache forced False whenever gradient_checkpointing is on at 48, and a kbit device map only when quantization is active at 49. That last detail is the difference between a QLoRA run that colocates quantized weights correctly across GPUs and one that silently double-loads.

The recipes are the repo’s true deliverables, and comparing them is a history of post-training itself. Zephyr-7B-beta’s SFT config points at Mistral-7B-v0.1 with flash_attention_2, a learning rate of 2e-5 for one epoch, sequences of 2048 tokens, and a per-device batch of 16 on the eight-GPU ZeRO-3 node declared in recipes/accelerate_configs/zero3.yaml - which sets zero_stage 3, zero3_init_flag, and zero3_save_16bit_model at lines 7-9; its DPO config then starts from the resulting Hub checkpoint with beta 0.01 and lr 5e-7, the low-beta regime the Zephyr report found best. The fsdp.yaml alternative chooses FULL_SHARD with TRANSFORMER_BASED_WRAP and BACKWARD_PRE prefetch - the same strategy family as the direct-preference-optimization reference - plus SHARDED_STATE_DICT and cpu_ram_efficient_loading. SmolLM3’s sft.yaml pushes the mixture API to its limit: 26 entries from smoltalk2 with weights like 0.02 for OpenThoughts3 reasoning traces and 0.5 for magpie-ultra, assistant_only_loss true, packing_strategy ffd at 65536 tokens, liger kernel enabled, cosine_with_min_lr at min_lr_rate 0.1, and a ddp_timeout of 18000 seconds because tokenizing that blend takes hours. SmolLM3’s DPO stage then runs loss_type apo_zero with beta 0.05 and padding_free true, while smollm2 shows the small-model contrast: beta 0.5, three epochs, tensorboard plus wandb. The Slurm launcher ties it together - it greps gradient_accumulation_steps out of the chosen config at line 90, reserves the last node as a vLLM server when use_vllm is set at 117-130, exports NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING at 133, and sruns the accelerate command across nodes at 140-167.

Release discipline rounds out the design. src/alignment/release.py keeps a REPLACE_PATTERNS table at lines 22-36 that rewrites the version string in four files at once - init.py, setup.py, CITATION.cff, and the README citation block - with pre_release_work at 73 refusing to patch from a dev branch at 77-78 and post_release_work at 95 bumping to the next dev0. setup.py carries the pinning that makes recipes reproducible: trl>=0.19.1, transformers>=4.53.3, torch>=2.6.0, peft>=0.16.0, deepspeed>=0.17.2, and liger-kernel>=0.6.0 among the deps at lines 43-73, with the package itself named alignment-handbook at version 0.4.0.dev0. It is a small thing until you try to reproduce a 2023 result on a 2026 stack - then the recipe that pins its world is the only one that still works.

From Install to a Replicated Zephyr

The README and scripts/README.md give a five-command path from nothing to a replicated Zephyr-7B-beta (commands abridged):

uv venv handbook --python 3.11 && source handbook/bin/activate
uv pip install torch==2.6.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126
uv pip install . && uv pip install "flash-attn==2.7.4.post1" --no-build-isolation
huggingface-cli login
# Stage 1 - SFT on 8 GPUs with ZeRO-3
ACCELERATE_LOG_LEVEL=info accelerate launch --config_file recipes/accelerate_configs/zero3.yaml \
  scripts/sft.py --config recipes/zephyr-7b-beta/sft/config_full.yaml
# Stage 2 - DPO from the SFT checkpoint
ACCELERATE_LOG_LEVEL=info accelerate launch --config_file recipes/accelerate_configs/zero3.yaml \
  scripts/dpo.py --config recipes/zephyr-7b-beta/dpo/config_full.yaml

Every parameter can be overridden on the command line - the docs suggest scaling batch size with GPU count to keep the global batch, and recipes will push straight to your Hub namespace by default.

Honest limits: the scripts are thin by design, so anything TRL does not expose - custom losses, curriculum scheduling, multi-stage reward modeling - means editing library code, not adding a config; the mixture API loads and concatenates full datasets in memory, which large blends only survive through the streaming-free weight trick it does not implement; the Slurm launcher is tuned for the Hugging Face cluster and says so; chat model evaluation leans on GPT-4 judges (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval) whose biases the README itself flags, including a taste for GPT-distilled models; and the repo is Apache 2.0 code wrapping libraries that move fast, so the exact torch, transformers, and trl pins are not suggestions - the recipes will silently change behavior without them.
entry.summary: A source tour of the Alignment Handbook: a thin TRL wrapper, the dataset mixture API, the Zephyr-7B-beta two-stage recipe, SmolLM3's 26-corpus blend, and the release tooling that ships models to the Hub.

entry.title: One YAML, Every Fine-Tune - Inside axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl

link.title: One YAML, Every Fine-Tune - Inside axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl

entry.content:
Fine-tuning an open model used to mean writing a training script: dataset glue, tokenizer surgery, trainer arguments, sharding flags, and a prayer that the checkpoint resumes. Axolotl replaces the script with a single YAML file and a codebase whose whole architecture exists to translate that YAML into a correct, memory-efficient training run. The result is one of the most widely used fine-tuning frameworks in the open-source world, and its source is a masterclass in how to layer configuration, data, and distributed training without letting any of them tangle. Version 0.21.1 under an Apache-2.0 license, it currently spans roughly 750 Python modules under its src tree, covering everything from classic Alpaca prompt formats to NVFP4 MoE LoRA kernels and asynchronous GRPO rollouts.

What makes the codebase worth reading is that it is honest about the messy parts. Every performance trick you have heard about - sample packing, flash attention swaps, FSDP2 with 4-bit bases, fused Liger kernels - lives here as an actual patch or plugin with clear seams, not as a blog diagram. You can trace one YAML key from the schema that validates it, through the loader that acts on it, to the trainer mixin that consumes it. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Overview: the CLI and config layer feeds dataset machinery and model loading; the trainer core consumes packed batches while patches and plugins reshape the model in between.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cli/main.py is the dispatcher whose main at line 529 wires every subcommand from train to preprocess to merge to cloud launches.
  • utils/config/init.py at 636 lines reads the YAML, applies defaults and plugin additions, and hands it to validation.
  • utils/schemas/config.py defines AxolotlInputConfig at line 196, a 2240-line pydantic schema that is effectively the framework’s contract with users.
  • utils/data/sft.py starts at prepare_datasets line 49 and assembles raw, tokenized, and shuffled datasets for supervised runs.
  • prompt_strategies/chat_template.py implements ChatTemplateStrategy at line 308, turning chat rows into masked label tensors.
  • utils/samplers/multipack.py provides MultipackBatchSampler at line 252, the best-fit-decreasing bin packer that keeps sequences together.
  • loaders/model.py is ModelLoader at line 209, 1468 lines handling quantization configs, device maps, and attention impl selection.
  • train.py closes the loop with train at line 703: setup, execute, save, model card, plugin teardown.

Why You Need This

If you have read our tours of peft, accelerate, or deepspeed, you know the individual parts: adapters, sharding, ZeRO stages. Axolotl is the orchestration layer that binds them behind one config file, and reading it shows you what integration actually costs. The repo does not just call PEFT’s get_peft_model; it patches PEFT’s parameter wrappers, seeds adapter initialization deterministically, and validates that a saved adapter matches the patterns you asked for. Those are the failure modes you only discover after your third night-long run dies at step 4000.

It is also the best available map of the 2025-2026 fine-tuning frontier in executable form. QLoRA on FSDP2 without a full-precision replica per GPU, NVFP4 MoE adapters via custom Triton kernels, selective activation checkpointing with CPU offload, asynchronous GRPO with a rollout producer - each landed as a self-contained module you can read in isolation. When a technique confuses you in a paper, the odds are good this repo contains the production version of it. Our torchtitan tour showed a clean-room trainer; axolotl shows the same ideas bolted onto the Hugging Face ecosystem where most practitioners actually live.

Finally, the plugin architecture is a lesson in extension design. Liger kernels, the ScatterMoE LoRA library, evaluation hooks, and even cloud launchers all enter through the same BasePlugin contract, getting called at pre-config-load, pre-model-load, post-model-load, and post-train phases. Nothing core knows Liger exists; the patch manager just asks registered plugins to do their worst at defined moments. If you maintain any training tool and want to stop merging every user request into core, this is the pattern to steal.

Detailed view: entry and config, dataset machinery, model and adapter loading, the trainer core, RL and preference trainers, and the patch and kernel layer.

Start at the entry, because the config is the product. cli/train.py defines do_cli at line 88 and do_train at line 37; the config path lands in utils/config/init.py which merges plugin-added keys before utils/schemas/config.py validates against AxolotlInputConfig at line 196. The schema is worth an evening: every knob from sequence_len to flash_attention is declared with types and defaults, and a capability-aware subclass AxolotlConfigWCapabilities at line 1939 cross-references the declared attention implementation against the installed hardware before a single GPU is touched. When validation fails you get a pydantic error pointing at the exact key, not a CUDA OOM nine hours later.

The dataset machinery is the second act. utils/data/sft.py loads raw datasets at line 319, applies the selected strategy through prompt_strategies/chat_template.py whose ChatTemplateStrategy at line 308 builds input and label tensors from any Jinja chat template, and persists the tokenized result so runs after the first skip straight to loading at line 268. The strategy ABCs live in prompt_tokenizers.py with PromptTokenizingStrategy at line 43, and the legacy Alpaca family at line 162 shows how train-on-input masking works. For RL runs the parallel module utils/data/rl.py at 528 lines prepares preference and prompt datasets instead.

The packing story is where axolotl earns its throughput. utils/samplers/multipack.py implements MultipackBatchSampler at line 252: sequence lengths come in, ffd_check at line 33 validates the bin estimate, pack_group at line 69 does best-fit-decreasing, and generate_batches at line 378 emits index batches whose padding waste is reported by efficiency at line 597. The sampler plugs into AxolotlTrainer through _create_multipack_sampler at line 363 of core/trainers/base.py, and the matching collator V2BatchSamplerDataCollatorForSeq2Seq at line 213 of utils/collators/batching.py pads to the batch max rather than a global max. A monkeypatch teaches the stock HF Trainer about these variable-length batches so loss normalization counts real tokens, a detail that silently skews results if ignored.

Model loading is a 1468-line negotiation with reality. ModelLoader.load at line 313 of loaders/model.py runs pre-model-load patches, picks device map via _set_device_map_config at line 922, quantization via _set_quantization_config at line 1006, and attention via _set_attention_config at line 1105, then _build_model at line 1243 actually constructs the model and _build_adapters at line 727 attaches LoRA through loaders/adapter.py whose load_lora at line 414 and find_all_linear_names at line 60 decide what gets adapters. The deepest magic is monkeypatch/accelerate/fsdp2.py: fsdp2_load_full_state_dict at line 183 shards a full checkpoint across ranks while keeping 4-bit quantized parameters intact, fsdp2_prepare_model at line 583 applies activation checkpointing, and the QLoRA companion monkeypatch/fsdp2_qlora.py makes adapters trainable on the sharded quantized base - the CPU-staged loading that lets you fine-tune models bigger than any single GPU.

On top sit the trainers and plugins. AxolotlTrainer at line 114 of core/trainers/base.py overrides compute_loss at line 771 for proper token-level normalization and composes mixins from core/trainers/mixins/packing.py. RL lives in core/trainers/grpo/trainer.py with AxolotlGRPOTrainer at line 57 and a context-parallel variant at line 89 whose _generate_and_score_completions at line 297 does the rollout-scoring dance, while core/trainers/grpo/async_trainer.py builds a full producer-consumer system - AsyncDataProducer at line 368, RolloutDataset at line 529, AsyncGRPOTrainer at line 832 - so generation overlaps training. Plugins enter through integrations/base.py; LigerPlugin at line 34 of integrations/liger/plugin.py swaps fused kernels in pre_model_load at line 114, and KernelsPlugin at line 146 of integrations/kernels/plugin.py routes MoE adapters to the ScatterMoE library’s grouped kernels while registering house Triton ops like the swiglu in kernels/swiglu.py.

What happens after the last step matters just as much, and the post-training exit ramps are built in. train at line 703 of train.py finishes with save_trained_model at line 274, which handles the FSDP merge-and-rename path (a helper at line 252 renames merged shards to adapter form), writes the model card at line 488, and calls PluginManager.post_train so plugins can unload or upload. From there the CLI takes over: cli/merge_lora.py collapses adapters into base weights with a memory-efficient variant at line 119, and the export command drives utils/gguf.py whose export_gguf at line 149 resolves llama.cpp binaries, preflights the vocab and template at line 89, and quantizes straight to a deployable GGUF for llama.cpp or Ollama.
